AK.key_factor: Mary Peltola finished first in the August top-four primary by eight points and led every October poll while outraising Dan S. Sullivan by more than two-to-one.
AK.reasoning: Peltola topped the August nonpartisan primary with 49.5% to Sullivan's 41.4%, raised $36.9M against his $14.1M, and led all six October polls by 1 to 7 points in a roughly D+9 national environment. However, Alaska's R+13.1 presidential baseline, ranked-choice transfers from minor Republican candidates, and late-October investigations into alleged spoiler-candidate recruitment involving Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. narrow her edge right before Election Day.

FL.key_factor: Ashley Moody leads every October poll in a state with a 1.5-million Republican voter registration advantage that Donald Trump carried by 13.1 points.
FL.reasoning: Despite a strongly Democratic national midterm environment, Moody has led in every poll since late September by 2 to 11 points, including a 50-44 lead in NYT/Siena and a two-point edge even in Angie Nixon's internal poll. Florida's substantial Republican registration advantage and Nixon's democratic-socialist profile limit crossover support enough for Moody to win comfortably.

IA.key_factor: Iowa's R+13.2 baseline and Ashley Hinson's slight edge across late-October polls barely offset Josh Turek's large fundraising and outside-spending advantage.
IA.reasoning: This open-seat race is a pure toss-up. Turek holds a $24.3M to $14.1M fundraising lead and a $20.2M to $4.8M outside-spending edge, helping him lead several early-October nonpartisan polls. However, Hinson is a disciplined incumbent representative in an R+13.2 state who led NYT/Siena, CNN/SSRS, Emerson, and almost every late-October survey, giving her the narrowest of edges.

KS.key_factor: Late-October nonpartisan polls show Adam Hamilton surging to a 3-to-9-point lead following scandals over Roger Marshall's past patient-billing lawsuits.
KS.reasoning: Although Kansas voted R+16.1 in 2024, Hamilton—a prominent suburban Kansas City pastor—is an ideal crossover recruit who outraised Marshall $19.2M to $7.5M. Revelations that Marshall sued over 700 medical patients, compounded by an October 20 rally controversy, damaged the incumbent severely; late-October polls from Emerson (+3), CNN/SSRS (+4), and Washington Post (+9) all put Hamilton ahead.

ME.key_factor: Troy Jackson leads in nine of twelve October polls and ties in the other three in a D+6.9 state during a strong Democratic midterm wave.
ME.reasoning: Unlike 2020, Susan Collins faces a working-class northern Maine populist in a midterm with an unpopular Republican president and a D+9 national environment. Following an October ProPublica report alleging a contractor pay-to-play arrangement, Collins has not led a single October poll, trailing Jackson in CNN/SSRS (+4), Marist (+2), Washington Post (+4), Suffolk (+2), and several Republican-sponsored surveys.

MI.key_factor: Abdul El-Sayed leads in nearly every October poll—including by 5 to 7 points in late-October surveys—backed by $53.8 million in candidate fundraising.
MI.reasoning: Despite $35.0M in Republican outside spending for Mike Rogers, El-Sayed's $53.8M fundraising haul and the strongly favorable national environment have put him ahead in 20 of 21 October polls. Late-October surveys from Rasmussen (+5), SSRS (+7), Mitchell (+7), and Glengariff (+6) confirm a clear and durable four-to-five-point Democratic advantage.

MN.key_factor: Peggy Flanagan leads every single poll in a blue-leaning state, including a 14-point lead in NYT/Siena and a 4-point lead in Michele Tafoya's own internal poll.
MN.reasoning: Minnesota has not elected a Republican senator since 2002, and in a strongly Democratic midterm year, sitting Lt. Gov. Flanagan has led first-time candidate Michele Tafoya across all 19 polls since September. Late-October surveys show Flanagan ahead by 7 points in KSTP/SurveyUSA, 14 points in NYT/Siena, and 3 to 4 points even in Republican partisan polling.

NC.key_factor: Popular former two-term governor Roy Cooper leads every poll by 8 to 14 points, prompting national Republicans to cancel $30 million in planned spending for Michael Whatley.
NC.reasoning: Cooper's statewide popularity, $49.6M to $13.7M fundraising dominance, and a $28.1M to $16.0M outside-spending edge have turned this open Republican seat into a rout. Cooper leads by roughly 9 to 11 points across nonpartisan and Republican polls alike, early voting shows heavy Democratic turnout, and the Senate Leadership Fund triaged Whatley's campaign in early October.

NE.key_factor: Incumbent Pete Ricketts leads in late-October polling—including a two-point lead in Dan Osborn's own campaign internal survey—in an R+20.5 state.
NE.reasoning: Independent union leader Dan Osborn makes Nebraska competitive just as he did in 2024 (losing by 6.7 points), aided by $35.1M in supportive outside spending. However, incumbent former governor Pete Ricketts holds a higher baseline than in 2024, leads 49-47 (and 50-48 two-way) in Osborn's own mid-October Impact Research internal poll, and benefits from Nebraska's deep-red partisan lean.

NH.key_factor: Chris Pappas has held a consistent 5-to-8-point lead at or above 50% in every poll since mid-September while outraising John E. Sununu four-to-one.
NH.reasoning: Pappas raised $23.7M to Sununu's $5.7M and benefits from a D+2.8 state in a D+9 national midterm environment. Every October poll—including Saint Anselm (+7), YouGov (+8), NPA (+7), and Rasmussen (+6)—places Pappas at 49% to 51% with Sununu stuck in the low-to-mid 40s and Constitution Party candidate Edmond LaPlante siphoning 2% to 4%.

OH.key_factor: Former three-term senator Sherrod Brown has raised $68.4 million and leads in 25 of 32 polls since September in a national environment roughly 10 points bluer than 2024.
OH.reasoning: Brown lost reelection by just 3.6 points in 2024 while Trump carried Ohio by 11.2 points. In a D+9 midterm wave, Brown's proven crossover brand, $68.4M to $19.9M fundraising advantage, and voter backlash over data-center tax breaks backed by Jon Husted have propelled Brown to consistent 3-to-6-point leads across Fox News, CNN/SSRS, Marist, Suffolk, and Cook Political polls.

SC.key_factor: South Carolina's R+17.9 partisan baseline gives appointed incumbent Darline Graham enough of a cushion to withstand Annie Andrews's massive fundraising lead.
SC.reasoning: After Lindsey Graham's death in July, newly appointed Sen. Darline Graham won a divisive August runoff and raised only $1.9M against Andrews's $24.2M, compressing the race to single digits. Still, Graham leads in most October polls (including ECU +4, Citadel LV +4, Trafalgar +3, and Targoz +1), and late-deciding conservatives in an inelastic R+17.9 Southern state should carry her over 50%.

TX.key_factor: After impeached Attorney General Ken Paxton ousted incumbent John Cornyn in the primary, James Talarico built a 7-to-1 total spending advantage and led 46 of 55 polls.
TX.reasoning: Paxton's primary defeat of Cornyn left Republicans with a uniquely polarizing nominee in a D+9 midterm wave. Talarico raised an extraordinary $146.3M (plus $31.3M in supportive outside spending) against Paxton's $22.3M (and $2.7M outside). Talarico leads in 46 of 55 polls—including UT, UH, TSU, NYT/Siena, Emerson, and Trafalgar—giving him a narrow edge despite Texas's R+13.7 baseline.

upset_watch.why: Josh Turek holds a $24.3M to $14.1M fundraising edge and a $20.2M to $4.8M outside-spending advantage while leading several high-quality nonpartisan polls in a D+9 wave environment.
